lessons.title: Mitigation and Carbon Accounting
lessons.mainIdea: Reducing emissions starts with counting them honestly, source by source, and the biggest sources are electricity, transportation, industry and agriculture.
reading: *Mitigation* means reducing the cause: cutting the greenhouse gases we add to the air. The first step is counting. Governments, companies and cities keep *greenhouse gas inventories*, ledgers that tally emissions by source. For the United States, the largest slices are transportation and electricity generation, each roughly a quarter to a third, then industry, then buildings and agriculture. Agriculture's share comes mostly from methane, which cattle produce as they digest, and nitrous oxide, which soil bacteria release from fertilizer. Both are far stronger heat-trappers per molecule than carbon dioxide.

Different gases are compared using *carbon dioxide equivalent*: the amount of carbon dioxide that would trap the same heat over a hundred years. Methane counts about 28 times its weight; nitrous oxide about 265. This lets a farm, a factory or a country add up everything into one number and track it over time. Illinois's inventory shows the state's emissions have fallen since the mid-2000s, mainly because coal plants closed and were replaced by natural gas, wind and existing nuclear plants.

A carbon footprint is the same accounting applied to a person or a product. The average American's footprint is among the highest in the world, roughly 15 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent per year, several times the global average. Where it comes from matters more than the total: for most households, the big items are driving, flying, home heating and electricity, and beef. Recycling and reusable bags are good habits, but they move the number very little compared with those four.

Mitigation options are ranked by cost per ton avoided. Some, such as efficiency improvements in buildings and switching from coal to wind, pay for themselves. Others, such as capturing carbon from the air, remain expensive. The world's emissions are still rising, though more slowly, and the gap between what countries have pledged and what the physics requires is large. Carbon accounting does not close that gap. It shows exactly where it is.

words.d: actions that reduce the causes of climate change, mainly by cutting greenhouse gas emissions
an accounting of a country's, company's or city's emissions, listed by source and gas
a way to express the warming effect of any greenhouse gas as the amount of carbon dioxide that would trap the same heat
the total greenhouse gases caused by a person, product or activity, usually measured per year

look.title: Carbon per Kilowatt-Hour, Over a Plant's Whole Life
look.cite: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, 2014, median life-cycle estimates, rounded
look.prompt: These figures include building and fueling each plant, not just running it. Which switch cuts the most carbon per kilowatt-hour, and why is that switch not free?

check.q: Why is methane from cattle counted as more than its weight in a greenhouse gas inventory?
choices: Because cattle produce so much of it
Because methane traps far more heat per molecule than carbon dioxide
Because it lasts longer than carbon dioxide
Because it is counted twice
check.why: Carbon dioxide equivalent scales each gas by its heat-trapping power; methane is about 28 times stronger over a century.

check.q: Which household change would reduce a typical American's carbon footprint the most?
choices: Driving and flying less and using less home energy
Switching to paper bags
Recycling more cans
Turning off lights in empty rooms
check.why: Transportation, home energy and beef dominate personal emissions; small habits matter far less by the numbers.

check.q: Illinois emissions have fallen since the mid-2000s mainly because
choices: the population decreased sharply
farms stopped using fertilizer
coal power plants closed and were replaced by gas, wind and nuclear
cars were banned in Chicago
check.why: Electricity generation shifted away from coal, the most carbon-intensive fuel, which lowered the state's inventory.

lessons.title: Adaptation
lessons.mainIdea: Because some warming is already locked in, communities must also adapt, redesigning buildings, farms and cities for the climate they will actually have.
reading: Even if the world stopped emitting tomorrow, the carbon dioxide already in the air would keep the planet warm for centuries. *Adaptation* means adjusting to changes that mitigation cannot prevent. It is not giving up; it is the other half of the job. A city that cuts its emissions and also builds a bigger storm sewer is doing both.

Chicago's Deep Tunnel is an adaptation project that began before anyone used the word. Since the 1970s the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District has bored more than 100 miles of tunnels hundreds of feet beneath the city, some 10 meters across. They hold stormwater until treatment plants can catch up. Giant reservoirs in old quarries hold billions of gallons more. The system was designed for the storms of the past century, and heavier rains now push it to its limits. So the city is adding green roofs, permeable pavement and rain gardens that soak water in where it falls.

Heat is the deadliest threat, and its adaptations are cheaper: trees. A shaded street can be 5 to 10 degrees Celsius cooler than a bare one on a hot afternoon. Mapping after the 1995 heat wave showed that deaths clustered in neighborhoods with few trees, more pavement and more isolated elderly people. Planting trees, painting roofs white, opening cooling centers and checking on neighbors are adaptation, and they save lives every summer. Farmers adapt too, with earlier planting, drought-tolerant seed, tile drains sized for bigger storms and cover crops that hold soil through a downpour.

Adaptation has limits. Sea walls protect a coast only up to the height they were built. A crop can tolerate only so much heat. And adaptation is unequal: wealthy places can afford tunnels and air conditioning; poor ones and poor countries often cannot, though they did least to cause the problem. Deciding who pays for adaptation, and how much warming to plan for, is a question science can inform but not answer alone.

words.d: adjusting buildings, farms, cities and habits to cope with climate changes that cannot be prevented
rain gardens, permeable pavement, green roofs and trees that manage stormwater and heat using natural processes
the tendency of a city, with its pavement and rooftops, to be hotter than the countryside around it, especially at night

look.title: Two Blocks in July
look.text: On one Chicago block, mature elms arch over the street, front yards are grass, and the roofs are light-colored. Four blocks away, the trees were cut for a road widening decades ago, the lots are paved for parking, and the roofs are black tar. On a 36-degree afternoon a thermometer on the second block reads several degrees higher, and at midnight the pavement is still radiating heat into the apartments above.
look.prompt: Which adaptations would make the biggest difference on the second block, and which are cheapest? Why might that block have fewer trees in the first place?

check.q: Why is adaptation necessary even if emissions are cut sharply?
choices: Because mitigation does not work
Because warming has already stopped
Because carbon dioxide already in the air will keep warming the planet for centuries
Because adaptation is cheaper than mitigation
check.why: Carbon dioxide lingers for hundreds of years, so some change is locked in regardless of future emissions.

check.q: What is the main purpose of Chicago's Deep Tunnel system?
choices: To supply drinking water
To carry trains under the river
To store stormwater during heavy rains until treatment plants can process it
To generate hydroelectric power
check.why: The tunnels and reservoirs hold combined sewage and stormwater that would otherwise overflow into the river and basements.

check.q: Why did deaths in the 1995 Chicago heat wave cluster in certain neighborhoods?
choices: Those areas had more trees
Those areas had fewer trees, more pavement and more isolated residents
Those areas were closer to the lake
Those areas had more air conditioning
check.why: Heat islands and social isolation made some neighborhoods far more dangerous, which points to trees and neighbor checks as adaptations.

lessons.title: Environmental Justice
lessons.mainIdea: Pollution and climate risk are not spread evenly; they fall hardest on low-income communities and communities of color, and environmental justice asks why and what to do about it.
reading: Hazel Johnson lived in Altgeld Gardens, a public housing development on Chicago's far South Side. She came to call the area a toxic doughnut: landfills, a sewage treatment plant, chemical factories and abandoned industrial sites on every side. Her husband died of lung cancer in 1969. She noticed how many neighbors had cancer, asthma and other illnesses, and she began going door to door with a survey. In 1979 she founded People for Community Recovery to fight for cleanup and for information about what was in the air, water and soil. She is often called the mother of the environmental justice movement.

*Environmental justice* is the principle that no group of people should bear a disproportionate share of environmental harms, and that everyone should have a voice in decisions that affect their environment. Study after study has found the same pattern Johnson saw: hazardous waste sites, highways, refineries and power plants are more likely to be located in low-income neighborhoods and in Black, Latino and Native communities. Sometimes the polluter came first and only cheap housing was left nearby. Often the neighborhood had the least political power to say no. Either way, residents breathe more particulate matter, live with more lead, and have higher asthma rates.

Flint, Michigan, showed how the pattern extends to water. In 2014 the city, under state-appointed emergency managers, switched its water source to the Flint River to save money and did not add the chemical that prevents pipes from corroding. Lead from old pipes leached into the tap water of a majority-Black city where much of the population was poor. Residents complained for more than a year before officials accepted the findings of outside scientists and a local pediatrician who showed that children's blood lead levels had risen. Lead causes permanent harm to developing brains. Chicago, which has more lead water service lines than any other American city, is replacing them slowly.

Climate change adds a layer. Heat waves kill in the neighborhoods with the fewest trees. Floods hit the low-lying areas where housing is cheapest. In 1994 the federal government directed agencies to consider environmental justice in their decisions, and Illinois now requires extra review and community notice for polluting facilities in already burdened areas. Science can map the burden. Deciding that the map is unacceptable is a choice a society makes.

words.d: the principle that environmental harms and benefits should be shared fairly and that affected people should have a say in decisions
out of proportion; a larger share than would be fair or expected
a lead pipe carrying water from the street main into a building, a major source of lead in tap water
adding chemicals to water so it does not dissolve metal from the pipes it flows through

look.title: A Federal Directive
look.text: Executive Order 12898, signed in February 1994, directed every federal agency to make achieving environmental justice part of its mission by identifying and addressing disproportionately high and adverse human health or environmental effects of its programs and policies on minority populations and low-income populations.
look.cite: Executive Order 12898, Federal Actions to Address Environmental Justice in Minority Populations and Low-Income Populations, 1994 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: This order asks agencies to identify and address unequal harms. What kinds of data would an agency need to collect to know whether a harm is disproportionate?

check.q: What did Hazel Johnson's door-to-door survey in Altgeld Gardens reveal?
choices: That the neighborhood had no pollution
That residents wanted more factories
That the area's air was cleaner than downtown
Unusually high rates of cancer, asthma and other illness in a neighborhood surrounded by polluting sites
check.why: Her survey documented a pattern of illness that matched the ring of landfills and factories around the development.

check.q: What caused lead to enter Flint's tap water in 2014?
choices: The city switched water sources without adding corrosion control, so lead leached from old pipes
The Flint River is naturally rich in lead
A factory dumped lead into the treatment plant
Residents installed new lead pipes
check.why: Corrosive river water without treatment dissolved lead from aging service lines into homes.

check.q: Which statement best describes the environmental justice pattern that research has found?
choices: Pollution is spread evenly across all neighborhoods
Polluting facilities are more often located near low-income communities and communities of color
Wealthy neighborhoods have the most landfills
Only rural areas face environmental harm
check.why: Studies consistently find that hazardous sites and heavy infrastructure cluster near communities with the least political power.

lessons.title: Policy Tools
lessons.mainIdea: Governments can reduce pollution by setting rules, putting a price on it, or creating tradable permits, and each tool has strengths the others lack.
reading: Suppose a state wants less sulfur dioxide from its power plants. The oldest tool is a *regulation*: a rule that says each smokestack may emit no more than a set amount, or must install a scrubber. Rules are clear and enforceable, and for something like lead in gasoline, where the goal is zero, they work best. Their weakness is that they treat every plant the same. A plant that could cut emissions cheaply has no reason to cut more than the rule demands, and a plant where cuts are very expensive must pay anyway.

A second tool is a *tax*: charge each ton of pollution. Now every plant has a reason to cut as much as it cheaply can, and the cheapest cuts happen first. Economists generally favor this because it gets the most reduction per dollar. Its weakness is that the total reduction is uncertain; you set the price and see what happens. Politically, taxes are hard to pass. A few places tax carbon; many more subsidize the alternatives instead, which is the tool the United States has mostly used for wind, solar and electric vehicles.

The third tool combines the two. In *cap and trade*, the government sets a total limit, the cap, and issues that many permits. Plants that cut cheaply can sell spare permits to plants that cannot. The total is guaranteed and the cheapest cuts still happen first. The 1990 Clean Air Act amendments used this for sulfur dioxide, and acid rain emissions fell faster and far more cheaply than industry had predicted. California and a group of northeastern states now run cap-and-trade markets for carbon dioxide. The risk is a cap set too loose, which makes permits nearly free and changes little.

Choosing a tool depends on the problem. Is the harm so severe that a hard limit is needed? Is the pollution easy to measure at the source? Are there many sources with very different costs? Are the public and lawmakers willing to see a price attached? Environmental science provides the first three answers; the fourth belongs to citizens, which is one reason to understand the tools well enough to argue about them.

words.d: a legally binding rule, such as a limit on emissions or a required technology
a policy that sets a total limit on pollution and lets companies buy and sell permits within that limit
a fee charged per ton of carbon dioxide emitted, meant to make polluting more expensive than cutting pollution
a government payment or tax break that makes a product or activity cheaper, such as credits for wind or solar power

look.title: Three Plants, One Goal
look.text: A state has three coal plants. Plant A can cut a ton of sulfur dioxide for 100 dollars, Plant B for 300 dollars and Plant C for 900 dollars. The state wants total emissions cut by 300 tons. A regulation orders each plant to cut 100 tons. A cap-and-trade system gives each plant permits and lets them trade.
look.prompt: Under the rule, what is the total cost of the 300-ton cut? Under trading, which plant will do the cutting and what happens to the total cost? Who might object to the trading result?

check.q: What is the main weakness of a one-size-fits-all emission rule?
choices: It cannot be enforced
It ignores that cutting pollution costs different amounts at different sources
It always sets the limit too high
It applies only to cars
check.why: A uniform rule forces expensive cuts at some plants while leaving cheap cuts undone at others.

check.q: In a cap-and-trade system, what is guaranteed?
choices: The price of a permit
That every plant cuts the same amount
The total amount of pollution allowed
That no plant pays anything
check.why: The cap fixes the total; trading lets the market decide who cuts and sets the permit price.

check.q: Which policy tool did the 1990 Clean Air Act amendments use to cut acid rain?
choices: A carbon tax
A ban on coal
Subsidies for scrubbers
A cap-and-trade market for sulfur dioxide permits
check.why: The acid rain program capped total sulfur dioxide and let plants trade permits, cutting emissions faster and cheaper than expected.

lessons.title: Costs, Benefits and Trade-offs
lessons.mainIdea: Every environmental decision trades one thing for another, and honest analysis puts numbers on both sides while admitting what cannot be priced.
reading: When the EPA proposes a new limit on soot, it must estimate what the rule will cost: scrubbers, fuel switches and higher electric bills. It must also estimate what the rule will gain: fewer hospital visits, fewer missed work days and fewer early deaths. This is *cost-benefit analysis*. Its retrospective studies of the Clean Air Act have found the health benefits outweighing the costs many times over. But the method requires assigning dollar values to things like a year of life or a clear view across the Grand Canyon, and reasonable people disagree about those numbers.

The heart of the problem is the *externality*: a cost that falls on someone who was not part of the deal. A coal plant sells electricity to its customers; the asthma downwind falls on people who bought nothing. Because the polluter does not pay that cost, it produces more pollution than it would if it did. Most environmental policy is an attempt to make the external cost internal, whether by rule, tax or permit, so the price of a thing reflects what it truly costs.

Trade-offs run in every direction. Cheaper electricity from coal means more mercury in fish. A wind farm displaces coal but kills some birds and bats and changes a landscape people love. Banning a pesticide protects streams but may raise food prices or push farmers to a worse chemical. Requiring corrosion control in Flint would have cost the city a few hundred dollars a day; skipping it cost hundreds of millions and a generation's health. Not every trade-off is close.

Two ideas help. *Risk assessment* asks how likely a harm is and how bad, so that a small chance of catastrophe is not weighed the same as a large chance of inconvenience. The precautionary principle says that when a harm could be severe and irreversible, lack of full certainty should not be a reason to delay action. Critics note that waiting for certainty is itself a choice with costs. The ozone case is the model: action came before the science was complete, the science firmed up, and the action was strengthened. Waiting would have been far more expensive.

words.d: comparing the total costs of a decision with its total benefits, usually in dollars, to judge whether it is worthwhile
a cost or benefit of an activity that falls on people who were not part of the transaction, such as pollution downwind of a factory
estimating how likely a harm is and how severe it would be, to guide decisions about it
the idea that when a possible harm is severe and irreversible, action should not wait for complete scientific certainty

look.title: Adding Up Clean Air
look.text: In its study of the Clean Air Act amendments, the EPA estimated that by 2020 the rules would prevent hundreds of thousands of premature deaths each year along with millions of cases of respiratory illness and lost work and school days, and that the dollar value of these benefits would exceed the costs of compliance by a wide margin, on the order of thirty to one under the agency's central estimate.
look.cite: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, The Benefits and Costs of the Clean Air Act from 1990 to 2020, 2011 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: A thirty-to-one ratio depends on how a prevented death is valued in dollars. What would change if that value were set much lower, and who should decide it?

check.q: What is an externality?
choices: A cost that falls on people outside the transaction, such as pollution downwind
The price of a product in another country
A tax on imports
The cost of building a factory
check.why: Externalities are costs or benefits not reflected in the price, which is why markets alone produce too much pollution.

check.q: Why do critics say cost-benefit analysis is hard to apply to environmental rules?
choices: Because costs are never measurable
Because it requires dollar values for things like health and scenery that people value differently
Because benefits always exceed costs
Because the EPA does not use it
check.why: Costs are usually clear; benefits like a life saved or a river restored must be converted to dollars, and that step is contested.

check.q: How does the ozone story illustrate the precautionary principle?
choices: Nations waited until the science was complete before acting
The problem solved itself
Action began before every detail was certain, and was strengthened as evidence grew
Scientists refused to recommend policy
check.why: The Montreal Protocol was signed when the mechanism was strong but not fully confirmed, then tightened as measurements came in.

lessons.title: Designing a Sustainable Community
lessons.mainIdea: A sustainable community is designed as a system, with energy, water, food, waste and transportation planned so the place can keep working for generations.
reading: *Sustainability* means meeting the needs of the present without using up the ability of future generations to meet theirs. That definition, from a 1987 United Nations report, sounds abstract until you apply it to a town. Where does its electricity come from, and will that source still be there in 50 years? Where does its water come from, and is the aquifer level falling? Where does its food come from, and is the soil holding? Where does its waste go? How do people get to work? A sustainable community is one where the honest answers to those questions do not point at a cliff.

The design tools are the ones this unit has built. Systems thinking maps the stocks and flows. Feedback loops show what will stabilize and what will run away. Life-cycle carbon accounting compares energy choices. Green infrastructure handles stormwater and heat. Walkable neighborhoods with transit cut the largest slice of a household's carbon footprint without asking anyone to give up going places. Buildings that are insulated and oriented to the sun use a fraction of the energy of ones that are not. Composting and recycling close material loops the way decomposers close them in a prairie.

Examples exist at every scale. Chicago's City Hall has grown a garden on its roof since 2000 to cool the building and soak up rain. A number of Illinois towns run on electricity from nearby wind farms. Communities from Copenhagen to Curitiba have built transit and bicycle networks that move most trips without cars. None of them is perfect, and each faced trade-offs: cost, space, the disruption of change, and the fact that people like the way things already are.

The last design principle is about who decides. Communities that planned with their residents, especially those in the most burdened neighborhoods, have generally built things that lasted. Environmental science supplies the evidence: the measurements, the mechanisms, the projections, the ranges. It cannot say how much a community should value a clean river against a lower tax bill, or the present against the future. Those are questions for citizens who understand the evidence well enough to argue from it. That, in the end, is why you learned this.

words.d: meeting present needs without reducing the ability of future generations to meet their own
adding up the environmental costs of a product or system from raw materials through use to disposal
describing a neighborhood where daily needs can be reached on foot or by transit rather than only by car
a system in which wastes become inputs, so little is thrown away, as in composting or a natural nutrient cycle

look.title: A Town on the Sangamon
look.text: A central Illinois town of 8,000 people gets electricity from the regional grid, water from the Mahomet Aquifer, and most of its jobs from farming and a grain elevator. Its downtown has emptied as stores moved to a highway strip. Heavy rains flood the same low neighborhood every few years. The town council has a modest budget and a survey showing residents want lower taxes, cleaner water and something done about flooding.
look.prompt: Using the tools from this unit, propose three changes the town could make. For each, name the stock or flow it affects, the trade-off it involves, and how you would know in ten years whether it worked.

check.q: Which definition of sustainability comes from the 1987 United Nations report?
choices: Using no resources at all
Growing the economy as fast as possible
Meeting present needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs
Returning to pre-industrial life
check.why: The Brundtland definition centers on fairness between present and future generations.

check.q: Why does a walkable neighborhood with transit reduce a household's carbon footprint so much?
choices: Because walking produces no carbon dioxide at all
Because it replaces the largest slice, transportation, without requiring people to travel less
Because transit is free
Because it eliminates home heating
check.why: Driving is among the biggest personal emission sources; design that cuts car trips addresses it directly.

check.q: What role does environmental science play in a community's decisions, according to this lesson?
choices: It decides how much a community should value the future
It replaces the need for public debate
It sets tax rates
It supplies the evidence and projections that citizens then argue from
check.why: Science can measure and predict; weighing values and trade-offs remains a choice for the community.

review.q: A temperature inversion is dangerous for air quality because
choices: it causes acid rain
it destroys ozone
it traps pollution near the ground under a layer of warm air
it makes cars burn more fuel
review.why: With warm air aloft, smoke and exhaust cannot rise and disperse, as happened at Donora and London.

review.q: Which pollution source has the Clean Water Act had the least success controlling?
choices: Factory discharge pipes
Sewage treatment plants
Oil tankers
Nonpoint runoff from farms and streets
review.why: The law's permit system targets identifiable pipes; diffuse runoff has no pipe to regulate.

review.q: What evidence confirmed that chlorine from CFCs was destroying Antarctic ozone?
choices: Aircraft flights measured high chlorine monoxide exactly where ozone was lowest
Ozone levels rose after CFCs were introduced
The hole appeared only over factories
CFCs were found to be poisonous
review.why: The 1987 expeditions found the reactive chlorine compound right where ozone was being lost, matching the predicted mechanism.

review.q: The Keeling curve shows carbon dioxide rising from about 315 parts per million in 1958 to over 420 today. What do ice cores add to this record?
choices: Proof that volcanoes cause the rise
Evidence that before industry the level was about 280 and had not been this high in hundreds of thousands of years
Evidence that the level was higher in 1800
Nothing, since ice cores measure temperature only
review.why: Trapped air bubbles in ancient ice show pre-industrial levels near 280 ppm and no comparable level in 800,000 years.

review.q: How do scientists attribute recent warming mainly to human activity?
choices: By assuming the sun cannot change
By measuring warming only near cities
Models with natural factors alone fail to reproduce warming since 1970; adding human greenhouse gases matches the record
By counting the number of hot days
review.why: Attribution rests on running models with and without human emissions and comparing them to observations.

review.q: Which is an example of adaptation rather than mitigation?
choices: Replacing a coal plant with wind turbines
Taxing carbon dioxide emissions
Insulating a home to use less heating fuel
Planting street trees to cool a neighborhood during heat waves
review.why: Adaptation adjusts to warming that will happen; the other three reduce emissions.

review.q: What happened in Flint, Michigan, in 2014 that made it an environmental justice case?
choices: A cheaper, corrosive water source was used without treatment, and lead poisoned a poor, majority-Black city while complaints were ignored
A factory explosion released chlorine gas
The city banned lead pipes
A drought dried up the city's wells
review.why: The harm fell on a community with little political power, and officials dismissed residents' evidence for over a year.

review.q: In cap and trade, why do the cheapest pollution cuts happen first?
choices: Because the government orders the cheapest plants to cut
Because plants that can cut cheaply profit by selling spare permits to those that cannot
Because permits are free
Because all plants must cut equally
review.why: Trading lets plants with low costs cut extra and sell permits, so the total reduction is achieved at the lowest overall cost.
